stories.title: As Malaysia's chip goals morph into a multi-state model, are they outgrowing Penang?
stories.summary: From Kedah manufacturing to Selangor design, multi-state ‘co-opetition’ is driving the country’s tech era
stories.content:
From Kedah manufacturing to Selangor design, multi-state ‘co-opetition’ is driving the country’s tech era

[KUALA LUMPUR] When AT&S, one of the world’s leading manufacturers of advanced circuit boards and integrated circuit (IC) substrates, was considering Malaysia for its next-generation substrate plant in 2020, Penang seemed to be the natural choice.

There was just one obstacle: finding a site large enough.

The Austrian electronics manufacturer instead crossed the state border to Kulim about 40 km away, where it secured the land, infrastructure and utilities needed for a plant that now produces IC substrates for AMD’s high-performance computing products.

stories.title: Dutch AI chip startup Euclyd raises $231 million in funding round co-led by Samsung
stories.summary: Dutch AI chip startup Euclyd has raised $231 million in a funding round co-led by Samsung, with former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink joining as chairman. The raise is among the larger early-stage financings for a European challenger in AI silicon.
stories.why_it_matters: Samsung's co-lead position signals strategic interest in diversifying AI chip exposure beyond Nvidia's ecosystem, while Wennink's appointment lends the startup deep credibility in semiconductor scale-up. The deal strengthens Europe's bid to remain relevant in AI hardware amid US-Asian dominance.
stories.content:
Dutch AI chip startup Euclyd has raised $231 million in a Series A funding round co-led by Samsung, Somerset Capital Partners, the Scaleup Europe Fund, and Innovation Industries.

The round also saw participation from EIFO, imec.xpand, the Brabant Development Agency, and Quadri, with the former president and CEO of ASML, Peter Wennink, joining Euclyd as chairman of the board.

Founded by Bernardo Kastrup and Atul Sinha in 2024 at Eindhoven’s High Tech Campus, the company describes itself as a “semiconductor systems company developing ultra-efficient infrastructure for foundation AI models.”

At present, the company is developing a platform that it claims will break through the “efficiency wall” that exists in current compute hardware to “transform AI inference economics.”

The platform consists of two elements, ‘craftwerk’ and CWS 32, which Euclyd claims are the world’s first agentic AI silicon and the world's lowest-power exascale AI factory, respectively.

In a statement, the startup said the financing will allow it to expand its engineering teams, accelerate its silicon and systems roadmaps, and prepare Euclyd for the commercial deployment of its offering.

“AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness, but its potential will remain constrained unless we fundamentally change the infrastructure beneath it,” said Kastrup, founder and CEO. “This financing accelerates our mission to make intelligence abundant through greater efficiency, lower cost per token, and broader access to advanced AI.”

stories.title: AVK launches dedicated funding arm to own and operate onsite power solutions for data center customers
stories.content:
On-site power generation developer for the data center sector, AVK, has launched a dedicated entity to fund and own on-site power infrastructure and deliver it directly to customers as a service.

AVK Capital is backed by the investment AVK secured from Partners Group last month. The Swiss private equity firm acquired a majority stake in AVK and said it intends to invest more than $1 billion of equity, backed by debt financing, to accelerate AVK’s expansion.

According to the company, it aims to provide data center developers and other industries with a route to a powered site without them having to carry the capital cost of the power infrastructure on their own balance sheets.

Under the new model, AVK will select and engineer the most preferential power solution for the site, including options such as microgrids, fuel cells, renewable integration, standby systems, and its own proprietary power solution, the AVK PowerPod.

AVK Capital will fund and own the infrastructure, with the developer purchasing energy via a long-term Power Purchase Agreement.

Ben Pritchard, CEO, AVK, said: “Access to power is the single biggest constraint on data center development in Europe, and the cost of solving it is the second. AVK Capital takes both off the table. We already design, build, operate, and maintain on-site power at commercial scale, and being able to fund and own it as well means a developer can contract for power in the same way they contract for any other service. That is what speed to power means in practice, and it is what the market has been asking for. No other business can bring the funding, the technology, and the delivery together under one roof the way AVK can.”

AVK launched its PowerPod system in April of this year, explicitly targeting the data center market. The unit comprises an engine for power delivery, switchgear, UPS, controls, and enclosures. According to the company, it can connect to the grid and operate completely off-grid, providing flexibility for data center customers looking to power their operations.

AVK touts a 2GW pipeline, and recently launched its first microgrid at a PureDC data center in Dublin, Ireland. The 110MW on-site microgrid, powered via natural gas engines, was billed at the time as Europe’s first large-scale microgrid.

The system comprises three interconnected energy centers, with each building generating up to 30MW of power. Energy Centre 1 (EC1) and EC2 will be fully operational by the end of 2026, followed by EC3 at a later stage.

stories.title: IQM sells second quantum computer to Japan's Toyo
stories.summary: The Spark system is expected to be operational in early 2027
stories.content:
Japan’s Toyo Corporation has purchased a second quantum computer from Finnish quantum firm IQM.

According to IQM Quantum Computers, the Spark system will be installed in Toyo’s R&D center in Kiba, Tokyo, and is expected to be operational in early 2027.

IQM’s Spark quantum computers have been specifically tailored for universities and research labs, offering high single-qubit and two-qubit gate fidelity, which the company says allows for reliable and accurate quantum applications. The systems come equipped with an “advanced cryogenic system” that operates at a temperature of about 20 millikelvin, close to absolute zero (-273.15°C or -459.67°F).

The news comes five months after Toyo announced it has purchased a 20-qubit Radiance quantum computer from IQM, a sale which reportedly represented the first enterprise quantum computer deployment in Japan. Installation of that system is planned for 2026 at the Global Research and Development Center for Business by Quantum-AI technology (G-QuAT), a research facility operated by the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) in Tokyo.

Toyo is a Japanese provider of advanced measurement solutions primarily across the automotive, energy, and ICT sectors. In a statement, the company said that once the systems are operational, they will be made available to domestic companies, organizations, research institutes, and universities. The two quantum computers will also serve as a testbed for evaluating and verifying components and technologies used in superconducting quantum computers.

The Japanese government is currently undertaking an ambitious project that is targeting 10 million domestic users of quantum technology and 50 trillion yen ($315bn) in quantum-generated production value by the end of the decade.

“What makes this purchase matter isn’t that Toyo bought a second system, it’s what they’re choosing to do with them,” said Jan Goetz, CEO and co-founder of IQM Quantum Computers. “That is the entire idea behind owning your own machine; you get to decide whom it serves. Japan has quantum goals to hit by 2030. You don’t get there with machines nobody else can touch; you get there because a company like Toyo chose to share access to the ones it now owns.”

Toshiya Kohno, representative director, president, and CEO at Toyo, added: “We believe that accelerating the adoption of quantum technologies requires environments where companies, universities, and researchers can gain hands-on experience with real quantum computers. By deploying IQM Spark at our R&D center and linking it with IQM Radiance 20, we will support a broad range of needs across different stages of quantum adoption, including talent development, technology validation, use case creation, and advanced research.”

Founded in Helsinki, Finland, in 2018, IQM brings full-stack quantum computers and applications to HPCs, research institutes, universities, and business enterprises. The company operates quantum data centers in Finland and Munich, Germany, offering cloud-based access to its systems. It has delivered quantum systems to supercomputing centers in South Korea, Poland, Italy, and Taiwan.

In July 2026, the company began trading on the Nasdaq, having completed its Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC) merger with Real Asset Acquisition Corp. (RAAQ).

stories.title: Nvidia’s Huang says AI industry doesn’t need any new laws
stories.summary: Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang dismissed the need for new artificial intelligence security regulations on Tuesday, arguing that market forces will help companies safely innovate.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Sept 16): Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang dismissed the need for new artificial intelligence security regulations on Tuesday, arguing that market forces will help companies safely innovate.

“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said during a Salesforce Inc. event. The CEO added that there’s a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast, reiterating a point he’s made previously.

“You can definitely have both at the same time,” he said during a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there.”

Huang’s company is the biggest maker of artificial intelligence accelerators — the chips at the heart of a massive data centre build-out — and he’s become one of the most prominent advocates for the broader AI industry. At an event earlier this week, he held an onstage phone call with President Donald Trump where they pushed back against recent arguments that AI development should be slowed.

AI risks have emerged as a hot-button issue in recent days, especially after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay proposing a slowdown. That followed the high-profile resignation of an Anthropic employee, who said the company and rival OpenAI were “gambling with our lives” because their technology could become a threat to humanity.

Huang said Tuesday that companies can decide not to release things that are harmful.

“Safety is paramount,” he said. “In a lot of ways, it’s job one. However, safety is an engineering problem.”

If we reach a point when “the company is out of control and the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right,” he said.
